newsitem.title: USA: Dow sets another record, dollar rises, bonds fall.
newsitem.headline: Dow sets another record, dollar rises, bonds fall.

text.p: U.S. blue-chip stocks hit record highs for the second straight day and the dollar rose again on Wednesday as Wall Street cheered fresh remarks on the economy and interest rates by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Bonds fell on profit-taking after the previous day's rally.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 26.71 points to a record 8,088.36, a day after soaring 155 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,714 to 1,152 on active volume of 616 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The latest reports of strong corporate earnings growth also propelled the market higher as Greenspan concluded his two-day report to Congress on the state of the economy.

During his testimony, Greenspan repeated his rosy moderate-growth, low-inflation appraisal of the economy and reinforced analysts' impression that the Fed was unlikely to raise short-term interest rates anytime soon.
"I think the die was cast yesterday," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "In effect, Greenspan has told us not to worry about the August or September Fed meetings."
Stocks surged early on Greenspan's comments but faded a bit when Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin later cautioned that it was a "close call" on whether short-term rates should rise.
Rivlin's comments tempered but failed to quash Wall Street's enthusiasm, given Greenspan's upbeat assessment of the economy.
"Alan Greenspan really rules the Fed," Wachtel said.

With their interest-rate worries allayed, investors were free to focus on corporate earnings, where the trend remained positive. Higher rates would tend to slow the economy and the growth of corporate profits, thereby hurting stock prices.

"There's no reason to buy stocks other than to participate in the earnings growth of the companies, and the second-quarter results have generally been coming in above consensus," said Al Goldman at A.G. Edwards & Sons.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury fell a quarter point, raising its yield to 6.43 percent from Tuesday's 6.41 percent, which was the lowest since early December. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar jumped in early trading, topping 1.83 German marks for the first time since August 1991. Overseas investors flocked to the dollar, attracted by buoyant U.S. financial markets.
The dollar ended at 1.8250 marks, up from 1.8245 marks on Tuesday. It rose to 115.68 yen from 115.00 yen.
Elsewhere, coffee prices jumped on rekindled concerns about a shortage of supplies for nearby delivery.
Coffee for September delivery jumped 12.55 cents to 181.65 cents a pound at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, bringing its gains to 22.8 cents a pound the last two sessions.
Gold prices slipped on talk of European central bank selling, August gold falling $2.20 to $323.80 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
September crude oil rose 15 cents to $19.63 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, Britain's FTSE 100 closed at 4,874.5, up 27.8 points, while Japan's 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,130.51, down 26.51 points.
